strengths: Gradient starvation analysis (Section 4.2) provides clear mathematical intuition for why MSE loss struggles with small velocities: ∂L_MSE/∂α = 2ρρ* sin α. This insight is well-articulated and motivates the proposed directional alignment elegantly.

Rigorous experimental validation with 3 random seeds, 37 total tasks (Adroit + Meta-World), proper statistical reporting with standard deviations, and comprehensive baselines (8 methods). Ablation study clearly shows impact of each component.

Meaningful improvements on challenging tasks: 9.4% on Medium Meta-World, 4.4% on Hard, 10.6% on Very Hard tasks. Shows that OMP particularly benefits high-precision manipulation where directional accuracy matters.

Training stability and convergence analysis (Figure 4) demonstrates OMP maintains higher and more stable performance during training compared to baselines, suggesting the added guidance mechanism is beneficial.
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 2 clearly contrasts different policy approaches). Well-organized structure and comprehensive experimental setup details (Section 5).
weaknesses: Contributions are incremental: cosine loss is standard in metric learning; finite difference approximation (Eq. 11) is elementary numerical analysis. Core novelty is limited—primarily combining existing techniques rather than introducing fundamentally new ideas.

Very similar to concurrent work DM1 (Zou et al., 2025) which also improves MeanFlow for robotic manipulation. The distinction (explicit directional alignment vs. dispersive regularization) appears narrow. Positioning relative to DM1 is insufficient.

Critical reproducibility gaps: (1) Hyperparameter values λ_Disp and λ_cos not specified anywhere in the paper. (2) Perturbation constant ε in DDE approximation (Eq. 11) described only as 'small' without actual value. (3) No hyperparameter sensitivity analysis. These omissions prevent reproduction and ablation of design choices.

DDE approximation introduces performance degradation (Table 2: -1.5% average). This undermines practical value of memory savings—practitioners must trade accuracy for memory. The paper doesn't provide actual memory consumption numbers, only claims of 'significant reduction.'

Improvements heavily skewed toward hard tasks: marginal gains on 21 easy Meta-World tasks (0-1.5%) which dominate the benchmark. Average improvement over MP1 is only 3.4%, and on easy tasks (21/34) it's near-zero.

Claims of 'few-shot generalization' are unsupported. Experiments use fixed 10-demonstration supervised learning datasets without actual few-shot adaptation or meta-learning. Title and abstract emphasize this but experiments don't validate it.

Lack of theoretical depth for DDE approximation: no error analysis, no discussion of validity conditions, no justification for the specific finite difference form. For high-precision robotic tasks, this is concerning.

Simulation-only evaluation with no real-world validation. No analysis of failure modes, task characteristics where cosine loss helps most, or sim-to-real transfer feasibility despite robotics application focus.

The geometric decomposition in Section 4.2 (u = ρn̂, u* = ρ*n̂*) assumes the ability to decompose error into orthogonal radial/tangential components but provides no formal justification for this decomposition.
Missing ablation on why -log((cos α + 1)/2) is the right cosine loss form. Other formulations of directional losses exist in literature but alternatives aren't discussed or compared.

strengths: Well-articulated gradient analysis (Section 4.2) identifying gradient starvation in MSE loss for low-velocity regimes with correct mathematical derivation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 37 tasks across Adroit and Meta-World with multiple random seeds and reported standard deviations
Particularly notable improvements on harder Meta-World tasks (9.4% on Medium, 10.6% on Very Hard) where more sophisticated approaches are needed
Clear presentation with helpful schematic diagrams (Figures 2-3) explaining the approach and experimental setup
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Cosine loss for directional alignment and finite-difference approximation (DDE) are standard techniques applied in straightforward manner; no comparison with concurrent work DM1 despite similar goals

Disconnect between theory and practice: Section 4.2 analyzes general high-dimensional MSE loss, but MP1 already uses MSE+Dispersive Loss; unclear why Dispersive Loss doesn't address directional problems and why cosine loss is necessary

Modest empirical improvements with statistical concerns: 3.4% overall improvement over MP1, only 1.5% on majority of tasks (Easy Meta-World); Figure 1 shows overlapping confidence intervals; no statistical significance testing provided

Unjustified DDE approximation claims: No actual GPU memory consumption numbers provided despite claiming 'significantly reducing memory'; Table 2 shows 1.5% performance drop with DDE, and epsilon value not specified anywhere

Incomplete ablation studies: Removing Lcos causes 3.7% drop vs. 0.6% for removing Ldis (Table 2), suggesting interaction effects not investigated; no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (λ values, epsilon)
Missing critical comparisons: No empirical evaluation against DM1 (concurrent work with similar motivation); limited explanation of why this approach is superior to alternatives

Notation and clarity issues: True mean velocity definition v₀ ≜ z_T - z₀ appears reversed; numerical stability of cosine loss when cos α → -1 not discussed; connection between gradient analysis and MP1's specific failures could be more explicit

Limited scope and reproducibility: Simulation-only evaluation; only 10 expert demonstrations per task; no code availability; incomplete hyperparameter specifications; approach specific to MeanFlow methods with unclear broader applicability

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical analysis in Section 4.2: Clear geometric explanation of gradient starvation in low-velocity regimes (∂L/∂α ∝ ρρ*) naturally motivates the directional alignment solution

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 37 robotic tasks across Adroit and Meta-World with proper stratification, multiple strong baselines, three random seeds, and ablation studies demonstrating component contributions
Practical and lightweight solutions: Both proposed modifications (Cosine Loss and DDE) are simple to implement without requiring architectural changes, making them accessible to practitioners
Stronger improvements on harder tasks where they matter: 9.4% improvement on Medium, 4.4% on Hard, and 10.6% on Very Hard Meta-World tasks, demonstrating effectiveness on challenging scenarios

Clear presentation and reproducible methodology: Well-structured paper with good motivations, clear figures (especially Figure 2), detailed experimental setup including convergence curves and training stability analysis
Ablation studies validate component contributions: Table 2 clearly shows directional alignment (Lcos) drives most improvements, with removal causing significant performance drops across tasks
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Cosine/directional losses are well-established in deep learning (metric learning, contrastive learning); DDE is standard finite difference approximation. The contribution is primarily engineering-focused rather than methodologically novel
Missing comparison with concurrent work: DM1 (Zou et al., 2025) addresses similar MeanFlow limitations but is not experimentally compared despite being highly relevant
Insufficient analysis of DDE-performance trade-off: Table 2 shows 1.5% performance drop with DDE, but no quantification of actual GPU memory savings or timing analysis to justify this trade-off
Hyperparameter sensitivity not addressed: Three new hyperparameters (λDis, λcos, ϵ) introduced with no ablation studies, missing exact values, and no guidance on how to set them for new tasks
Statistical rigor gaps: No significance testing despite reported standard deviations; confidence intervals overlap for some comparisons; claims like 'fastest convergence' lack quantitative support

Gradient starvation analysis lacks empirical validation: While geometric explanation is correct, no evidence that this is the actual limiting factor in MP1 vs. other potential issues (data diversity, network capacity)
Limited experimental scope: Only simulation tested; no real robot validation despite claims about 'real-time deployment' and high-precision manipulation; transfer to real robots unknown
Missing implementation details: Exact hyperparameter values not provided; selection of ϵ in finite difference not explained; code availability not mentioned

Incomplete related work: No justification for Cosine Loss over other directional losses (triplet, contrastive); limited discussion of directional alignment in other flow-matching methods; recent variants (World4RL, MTDP) mentioned but not compared
Figure 1 interpretation concern: Claimed advantage over MP1 is visually subtle with overlapping error circles; visual distinction between methods is unclear despite numerical improvements

strengths: Clear and rigorous mathematical analysis of MeanFlow pathologies, particularly Spectral Bias (Theorem B.1) and Gradient Starvation, providing useful insights into method limitations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning 14 Adroit tasks, 50 Meta-World tasks, and real-world validation with proper ablation studies and multiple random seeds
Consistent performance improvements across diverse benchmarks (3-10% range), demonstrating robustness of the approach
Practical solutions with clear engineering trade-offs documented (JVP vs DDE variants showing memory-accuracy trade-offs in Table 3)
Strong reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, training stability analysis, and sensitivity studies across temporal scales
weaknesses: Theoretical contributions are incremental—identified pathologies are expected consequences of MeanFlow formulation, and proposed solutions (alignment loss, finite-difference approximation) are straightforward engineering fixes rather than novel techniques
Improvements are modest and lack clear guidance on when OMP is preferable; ablation study shows Directional Alignment removal causes only ~1.2% drop on Adroit, questioning its necessity

Limited experimental scope restricted to visual manipulation tasks; unclear generalization to other domains; real-world evaluation limited to 3 tasks without comprehensive comparison to recent methods like iFlow or PointMapPolicy

Insufficient analysis of individual component contributions; unclear which solution (alignment vs memory optimization vs composite loss) drives most improvements, or how they jointly address all three identified pathologies

Missing theoretical justification for DDE approximation validity—when ε-perturbation is appropriate is not established; memory analysis doesn't account for modern techniques like gradient checkpointing that could mitigate overhead

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 13 simulation and 3 real-world tasks, including proper ablations and multiple baselines
Identifies specific limitations of MeanFlow (spectral bias, gradient starvation, memory complexity) with supporting mathematical analysis
Demonstrates consistent improvements across diverse manipulation benchmarks (Table 1) and training stability (Figure 5)
Includes real-world validation on physical robotic tasks, establishing practical applicability
Well-documented experimental setup with detailed hyperparameters and supplementary analysis in appendices
weaknesses: Theoretical analysis is incomplete and not rigorous: Claims about spectral bias and gradient starvation are suggestive but lack formal proofs. The connection between low-pass filtering and the need for directional alignment is assumed rather than proven

The proposed solution (Directional Alignment) is ad-hoc and trivial: Adding a cosine similarity loss (Eq. 12) is an obvious engineering fix that doesn't justify the title of a research contribution. No principled justification for why this specific approach is optimal
Theory-practice disconnect: The theoretical analysis (Section 4.2) doesn't clearly motivate Directional Alignment as the correct solution. Why not alternative approaches?

Synthetic experimental setup is circular: The 'Sum of Sines' velocity field (Section C.1) is specifically constructed to demonstrate the problem, not discovered empirically in real robot data. Figure 2 uses synthetic data, not actual Adroit/Meta-World tasks

Empirical improvements are modest: 2-5% gains over MeanFlow on most tasks (Table 1) and 3-15% on real-world tasks. For a top-tier venue, these incremental gains combined with weak theory are insufficient
Limited evaluation scope: All tasks are dexterous manipulation with point clouds. No evaluation on other robotics domains or with alternative generative policy paradigms (diffusion, etc.)

Significant unexamined design choices: The composite loss (Eq. 13) with three terms appears ad-hoc. Loss weight sensitivity is not analyzed. The DDE approximation uses ε=1 without justifying this choice or analyzing approximation error
Memory-accuracy trade-off under-explored: Table 3 shows DDE reduces memory but degrades accuracy significantly (82.3±1.7% → 80.8±2.2%). The practical utility of this trade-off is unclear

Limited novelty: Directional alignment is a straightforward addition of a standard loss function. DDE is a basic finite-difference technique. The work is primarily engineering refinement of existing MeanFlow method

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis identifying three specific pathologies (spectral bias, gradient starvation, memory complexity) in applying MeanFlow to robotic manipulation, with formal mathematical treatment (Theorem B.1 on low-pass filtering, polar decomposition analysis of gradient dynamics)

Well-motivated and targeted solutions: Directional Alignment (Eq. 12) directly addresses gradient starvation by decoupling magnitude and direction; DDE approximation (Eq. 14) reduces memory overhead from O(2M_std) to practical levels

Comprehensive experimental validation combining simulation benchmarks (37 tasks across Adroit/Meta-World) with real-world robot demonstrations, showing consistent 3-4% improvement over strong baselines including MPI and FlowPolicy

Solid reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters (Table 4), multiple random seeds (3 simulation, 20 real-world), ablation studies (Table 3, Table 5) that systematically isolate component contributions, and code availability promised

Clear presentation with effective motivation (Figure 1), intuitive schematics (Figure 3), well-organized structure from problem formulation through methods to comprehensive experiments, and detailed appendices
Practical significance: enables real-time diffusion-based robotic manipulation previously limited by latency, achieving 82.3% on Meta-World vs. 78.9% for MPI while maintaining efficiency
weaknesses: Critical technical detail underspecified: perturbation constant ε in DDE approximation (Eq. 14) lacks selection justification and sensitivity analysis, limiting reproducibility despite otherwise detailed experimental setup
Limited theoretical guarantees: gradient starvation analysis in Section 4.2.2 is observational rather than providing convergence proofs for Directional Alignment learning dynamics

Composite loss balance not thoroughly analyzed: Equation 13 combines three terms with hyperparameters λ_DDE and λ_DA, but sensitivity to their relative magnitudes is only briefly addressed through Table 3 ablations without detailed weighting investigation

Incremental novelty over MeanFlow: primary contribution is identifying problems with existing method and proposing targeted fixes; DDE is essentially first-order Taylor approximation (standard technique), and directional decomposition concept exists in other domains
Modest empirical improvements: 3-4% average gain over strong baselines, with only 0.7-1.1% on Meta-World Easy tasks—consistent but not transformative, potentially limiting practical significance
Real-world validation limited to simple manipulation tasks (pick/place, cleaning table, slip ring); performance on complex assembly or high-precision manipulation remains unexplored

Missing practical guidance: no wall-clock training time comparisons, limited discussion of when practitioners should prefer OMP vs. MeanFlow, computational feasibility for resource-constrained scenarios unclear
